source: Gopnik & Wellman (2012; 2014 author manuscript) Reconstructing constructivism: causal models, Bayesian learning mechanisms, and the theory theory
finding: Core theory. Children hold abstract causal theories that work like causal Bayes nets. Learning is Bayesian updating over structured hypotheses. An intervention fixes a variable and cuts its incoming arrows (graph surgery), so seeing and doing give different predictions. Counterfactuals are formally the same as interventions.
numbers: Review, no new data. Psych Bull 138(6):1085-1108.
quote: you still have to decide which hypotheses to evaluate, and equally which evidence to gather
limits: The authors name the main drawback: Bayes scores given hypotheses but does not say which hypotheses to generate or which evidence to gather.
agent_relevance: Formal frame for S4 TEST: a test is an intervention chosen to split live hypotheses. Hypothesis generation is the open problem, and it is the agent's weak point.

source: Gopnik, Sobel, Schulz & Glymour (2001) Causal learning mechanisms in very young children (blicket detector); read only through Gopnik & Wellman review
finding: Paradigm: a blicket detector lights and plays music when some objects are placed on it. Children saw B alone fail, A alone work, and A+B work. Only 'A is a blicket, B is not' fits. Ages 2, 3 and 4 then chose to add only A to start it and remove only A to stop it. They inferred structure from covariation, then used it to plan interventions.
numbers: Ages 2, 3, 4. Exact pass rates not read; primary paper not opened.
limits: Second-hand through the review. Deterministic task. Take sample sizes and rates from the primary before citing.
agent_relevance: Shows the loop the schema needs: infer structure from data, then pick the test or action that follows from the inferred structure.

source: Sobel, Tenenbaum & Gopnik (2004) Children's causal inferences from indirect evidence: backwards blocking and Bayesian reasoning in preschoolers; read only through Gopnik & Wellman review
finding: Backward blocking. A alone activates the machine, then A+B activates it. Children judge B less likely to be a blicket, using trials where B was never alone. The inference is probabilistic and hard for simple associative accounts. Children also used stated base rates: if blickets were rare they said B was a blicket less often than if blickets were common (also Griffiths, Sobel, Tenenbaum & Gopnik 2011). Sobel & Kirkham (2007) report similar looking-time patterns from 18 months.
numbers: Preschool children. Rates not read; primary not opened.
limits: Second-hand. Sobel & Munro (2009, 3-year-olds) asked whether the result is backward blocking or recovery from overshadowing; not opened.
agent_relevance: A clean test of explaining away: a sufficient early cause lowers belief in a rival cause. The agent should lower a hypothesis when another cause already explains the data.

source: Gopnik, Glymour, Sobel, Schulz, Kushnir & Danks (2004) A theory of causal learning in children: causal maps and Bayes nets; read only through Gopnik & Wellman review
finding: Children combined interventions and statistics to infer which way a causal arrow points (A causes B or B causes A). Schulz, Gopnik & Glymour (2007) extended this: 4-year-olds told a causal chain from a common cause using patterns of dependence and intervention.
numbers: Exact numbers not read.
limits: Second-hand. This is the paper that proposed the causal-map view; primary not opened.
agent_relevance: Direction of a link needs an intervention, not only correlation. Matches Corr2Cause failures in LLMs (see later lines).

source: Kushnir & Gopnik (2005); Schulz & Somerville (2006): causal strength and hidden causes; read only through Gopnik & Wellman review
finding: 4-year-olds treated a block that set off the machine 2 of 3 times as more effective than one that set it off 2 of 6 times, though both set it off twice. Schulz & Somerville: a machine that went off only 2 of 6 times led children to infer a hidden extra variable.
numbers: 2/3 versus 2/6 contrast. Group sizes not read.
limits: Second-hand through review.
agent_relevance: Failure rate carries information. A test that fails sometimes should raise the possibility of a hidden factor, not only lower belief.

source: Schulz & Gopnik (2004); Schulz, Bonawitz & Griffiths (2007): priors versus evidence, as described in the Bonawitz et al. chapter
finding: Preschoolers heard two stories where a candidate cause A co-occurred with an effect in ABE, ACE, ADE patterns. In one story all variables were in one domain; in the other, A was a psychological cause of a biological effect. Evidence raised choice of A over baseline in 4-year-olds. All children chose A more within domain than across domains, so theory (prior) and evidence both mattered. The share of children choosing A matched the Bayesian posterior: about 80% chose A when the model said 80%.
numbers: Posterior-matching is a group-level share of children. Exact N not given in the chapter text.
limits: A group-level match does not show each child holds a posterior; this is why the sampling hypothesis was proposed.
agent_relevance: Evidence plus prior, not evidence alone. A cross-domain cause needs more data than a same-domain cause, so the agent's priors should be explicit.

source: Denison, Bonawitz, Gopnik & Griffiths (2013) Rational variability in children's causal inferences: the Sampling Hypothesis. Cognition 126:285-300. Experiment 1
finding: Children guessed which block (red or blue) had fallen into a machine. Guesses matched the probability of each colour (probability matching), not always the likely colour (maximizing) and not 50/50. Guesses were also dependent over time: with no wait children often alternated, a pattern independent sampling would not give. After a 1-week delay between trials the dependence weakened.
numbers: Bag with 20 red and 5 blue blocks (4:1). 40 children aged 4-5, 20 per condition (short wait, long wait). 28 of 40 trials (70%) chose the more probable colour, binomial p=.017 vs chance, not different from 80% (p=.175). Short vs long wait distributions differ, chi-sq(7,N=40)=22.3, p=.002. Each differs from a flat distribution: long wait chi-sq(7,N=20)=33.91, short wait 77.75, both p<.001. Dependency: Fisher exact p<.001 (short wait), p=.029 (long wait). Without two outlier children the long-wait fit was marginal, chi-sq(6,N=18)=12.7, p=.09.
quote: children's guesses matched the probabilities resulting from this process rather than the overall frequency of different colors
limits: Alternating may reflect children giving a new answer when an interviewer repeats a question (a known social effect, which the authors discuss). Memory noise cannot be fully ruled out in Exp 1.
agent_relevance: Repeated sampling from one source gives dependent, not independent, answers. Supports G4: do not treat repeated samples as independent evidence.

source: Denison et al. (2013) Experiment 2: varying proportions
finding: Three groups tested whether guesses scale with the true proportion. The share of majority-colour guesses rose with the ratio, as probability matching predicts. A noisy-maximizing model fitted worse. A logistic regression found a linear rise of choices with log odds.
numbers: 75 children aged 4-5, 25 per condition: 95:5, 75:25, 50:50 (the 80:20 data of Exp 1 added to the regression). 95:5: majority colour on 21/25 trials (84%), above chance p<.001, not different from 95% (p=.07). 75:25: 15/25 (60%), not different from 75% (p=.14 in text). 50:50 at chance. The noisy-max model needed about 58% pure chance responding to fit. 8 extra children excluded (sibling interference 2, failed comprehension check 6).
limits: Small cells: 25 children, one test trial each. The 75:25 group (60%) was below the prediction, which the authors credit to low power.
agent_relevance: A system that samples hypotheses in proportion to belief shows graded variability. This is a model of why diverse attempts help.

source: Denison et al. (2013) Experiment 3: three colour hypotheses
finding: With three colours (chance 33%), children still gave graded guesses, which moved toward the predicted proportion but undershot for the flatter bag.
numbers: 100 children aged 4-5, 50 per condition. 82:9:9 bag: majority colour on 36/50 (72%), above 33% chance p<.001, not different from 82% (p=.11). 64:18:18 bag: 24/50 (48%), above chance but different from the expected 64% (p=.03). Between conditions chi-sq(1,N=100)=5.06, p=.025.
limits: The 64:18:18 group undershot matching: a boundary where a noise parameter blurs matching.
agent_relevance: Matching is noisy and drifts toward uniform when options are many; expect more spread with a wide hypothesis space.

source: Denison et al. (2013) Experiment 4: combining priors and likelihood across two bags
finding: Children had to combine the 50% chance of each bag being picked with the chance of a colour inside that bag. The more numerous colour overall was less likely to be in the machine. Children's guesses matched the combined probability, not the raw colour frequency.
numbers: 33 children aged 4-5. Separate-distributions condition (bag 1: 14 red, 6 blue; bag 2: 2 blue; combined P(blue)=65%): 20 children chose the less numerous colour on 26/38 trials (68%), not different from the predicted 65% (p=.798), above 50% (p=.034), different from the frequency-match prediction of 36% (p<.001). Merged control, 13 children: 24/36 (67%) vs predicted 64% (p=.886). Only 10 of the 20 children completed all three trials.
limits: Small N, uneven trial counts because the multi-toy method was added part way through data collection.
agent_relevance: Nested uncertainty (which source, then which item) was combined by 4-year-olds. LLMs often fail this; see Binz & Schulz and Qiu et al. below.

source: Bonawitz, Gopnik, Denison & Griffiths (2012) Rational randomness: the role of sampling in an algorithmic account of preschooler's causal learning. In Xu & Kushnir (Eds) Rational Constructivism in Cognitive Development, pp 161-192
finding: Frames the algorithm problem (Marr): full Bayes needs every hypothesis scored, which is too costly. Proposal: children sample a few hypotheses from the posterior (Monte Carlo). Reviews the sampling data, then Win-Stay Lose-Shift algorithms, MCMC and particle filters. Variability in answers is read as a signature of sampling, not noise.
numbers: Chapter repeats bag results: red chip guessed on 70% of trials for the 4:1 bag; 72% (82:9:9) vs 53% (64:18:18); in the two-bag case 32% red, against a 35% posterior prediction and a 64% frequency prediction.
limits: The algorithm-level claim is indirect: matching behaviour fits sampling, but other mechanisms could give it. The chapter says more work is needed to separate algorithms.
agent_relevance: Design hint: hold a small set of live hypotheses, draw from them in proportion to credence, and let tests (not opinions) move the weights.

source: Bonawitz, Denison, Gopnik & Griffiths (2014) Win-stay, lose-sample: a simple sequential algorithm for approximating Bayesian inference, as reported in the Bonawitz chapter
finding: A one-hypothesis-at-a-time learner keeps its hypothesis while data fit and resamples from the posterior with a probability tied to the likelihood of the latest datum. A proof shows this approximates Bayesian inference. In a probabilistic block task, children's step-by-step guesses fitted WSLS better than independent sampling.
numbers: Task: red block activated the machine 5 of 6 times, green 3 of 6, blue 1 of 6. A mystery colourless block was tested several times and children guessed its colour after each result. Aggregate guesses correlated highly with Bayesian posteriors. WSLS had higher log-likelihood than independent sampling. Exact correlations and N not given in the chapter text.
limits: Chapter summary of work reported elsewhere; the published paper was not opened. Hypothesis space was small (three colours).
agent_relevance: WSLS is a cheap loop for the schema: stay with the current hypothesis until a failing test, then resample. Fits G1 (doubt only on a signal) and G2 (revise from real output).

source: Lucas, Bridgers, Griffiths & Gopnik (2014) When children are better (or at least more open-minded) learners than adults. Cognition 131:284-299. Experiment 1
finding: Hierarchical Bayes. After training on a conjunctive machine (needs two blickets), 4-year-olds applied the conjunctive rule to new objects more than adults did. In the disjunctive condition both groups behaved alike. Adults carry a stronger prior for disjunctive rules and update less.
numbers: 32 children (mean age about 4.5), 16 per condition; 88 conjunctive and 55 disjunctive adults (5 excluded). Children, disjunctive: F=1.5 of 2, D=.38, E=.50. Children, conjunctive: F=1.63, D=1.31, E=.75 (D vs F not different, p=.51). Adults, conjunctive: F=1.52, D=.47 (D called non-blicket more than half the time, t(82)=6.269, p<.001). Children rated D a blicket more than adults, first repetition .63 vs .22 (Fisher exact p=.0019); E .44 vs .05 (p<.001).
limits: Adults also moved a little toward conjunctive (p=.0031), so the gap is one of degree. One-tailed tests for planned contrasts.
agent_relevance: A strong prior can block a well-supported unusual rule. The agent must not let a default hypothesis override a clean test result.

source: Lucas et al. (2014) Experiment 2: baseline and interventions
finding: Added a baseline condition and asked which objects participants would use to activate the machine, to rule out wording effects of 'blicket'. Children's actions matched their judgements, so the difference was a belief difference.
numbers: Children in the conjunctive group chose interventions including D in 20 of 25 (p=.002) and multiple objects in 21 of 25 (p<.001); in the disjunctive group 3 of 25 chose D and none chose multiple objects. Baseline children: D .42, E .33, F .75. Adults conjunctive: D .25 vs E .11 (p=.22); D versus the disjunctive and baseline groups p=.29 and p=.14; most adults activated with F alone. Group sizes of 28, 28 and 26 are reported for one age group (text unclear which).
limits: Single lab, Berkeley, with a stated low base rate of blickets.
agent_relevance: Behaviour (interventions) confirms stated belief; score actions, not words (G2).

source: Lucas et al. (2014) Experiment 3: adult language control (tulver flowers)
finding: Changing the cover story from blickets to flowers that make a bear sneeze did not remove the adult disjunctive bias.
numbers: 27 adults. 25 of 27 called flower F a tulver flower and none called D one (p<.001). On the intervention question 21 of 27 would remove only F.
limits: College-student adults only.
agent_relevance: Priors are domain-general habits; an LLM trained on text may carry the same habit.

source: Gopnik, Griffiths, Lucas and colleagues (2017) Changes in cognitive flexibility and hypothesis search across human life history from childhood to adolescence to adulthood. PNAS 114(30):7892
finding: Same blicket task across ages. Preschoolers adopted the unusual hypothesis most readily, then school-age children, then adolescents and adults. Older learners prefer a familiar hypothesis even when it fits the new evidence less well. In a social-domain task, preschoolers and adolescents were the most flexible.
numbers: New samples: 6-7 years n=90, 9-11 years n=90, 12-14 years n=86; 240 adults online in the social task. Preschoolers and adults taken from Lucas et al. Exp 2. Exact percentages are in figures, not extracted.
limits: Cross-sectional design. The authors read the trend as a shift from exploration to exploitation; there is no within-person test. The adolescent U-shape appears only in the social task.
agent_relevance: Supports a temperature idea: keep hypothesis search wide early, narrow later; fits an explore-then-commit state order.

source: Schulz & Bonawitz (2007); Cook, Goodman & Schulz (2011): children choose informative tests; read only through Gopnik & Wellman review
finding: Given a toy with two levers and two effects, children who saw a confounded demonstration (both levers at once) explored the old toy more than a new one, while children who saw clear separate effects switched to the new toy. In the confounded condition they later showed they had worked out how the toy worked.
numbers: Ages 3-4 in Schulz & Bonawitz; group sizes and rates not read.
limits: Second-hand. The review itself says play is not optimal experiment design, only systematic enough to give causally relevant evidence.
agent_relevance: Core of S4: pick tests that remove confounds. Detect ambiguity by checking whether two hypotheses predict the same outcome, then test where they disagree.

source: Kosoy, Collins, Chan, Huang, Pathak, Agrawal, Canny, Gopnik & Hamrick (2022) Learning causal overhypotheses through exploration in children and computational models. CLeaR 2022
finding: Online blicket machine. Children aged 4-5 explored freely. Being told the possible rule types (given hypothesis) made exploration far more informative. Exploration did not look like plain information gain or reward maximising.
numbers: N=85 children aged 4-5 (20-23 per condition). Data sufficient to disambiguate the hypothesis space: 71% given-hypothesis vs 32% not-given (two-proportion z, p=.002). Mean actions in Table 1: conjunctive not-given 12.2, given 12.68; disjunctive not-given 8.95, given 15.4. 17.7% and 17.5% tested the machine with no object; about 65-67% tried a different order of the same objects.
limits: Exploratory proof of concept at a science museum; not a representative sample.
agent_relevance: Knowing the space of possible rules makes tests much more efficient. Give the agent an explicit hypothesis space before testing (S4).

source: Kosoy, Chan, Liu, Collins, Kaufmann, Huang, Hamrick, Canny, Ke & Gopnik (2022) Towards understanding how machines can learn causal overhypotheses. arXiv 2206.08353
finding: Blicket environment tested deep RL, behaviour cloning, decision transformers, GPT-3 (text-davinci-002) and PaLM. Deep RL did not generalise to held-out overhypotheses. Language models, given the observations children got, picked the right machine type when hypotheses were given but struggled when they were not, and could not express uncertainty about structure. GPT-3 over-named blickets. Chain of thought did not help PaLM.
numbers: Decision transformer reward on the blicket quiz (+1/-1): 0.16 with random pretraining vs 2.37 with 15 forced exploration steps; forced-choice accuracy 0.67 to 0.77. Behaviour cloning reward stayed between -0.16 and 0.22. Language model results given as counts over a few prompts (e.g. PaLM two-shot not-given: 7 wrong), not rates.
limits: Tiny prompt set; 2022 models only. GPT-3 temperature 0.7, PaLM greedy.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that LLMs lack calibrated uncertainty over rule types and under-explore. Argues for code-held hypothesis sets (G5).

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3. PNAS; arXiv 2206.14576
finding: GPT-3 solved a blicket vignette, an intervention vignette and a counterfactual pill problem like people. Small changes broke it: in the cab problem it said 20% for a black cab when 15% were blue and 85% green. In a seeing-versus-doing task it did not show the human split between observation and intervention. The authors say it fails miserably in causal reasoning tasks.
numbers: 12 vignettes: 6 answered correctly, all 12 correct or human-like errors, but adversarial variants broke them. Blicket vignette: first object a blicket, second not (correct). Waldman & Hagmayer design: 20 observations, then do(B) queries.
limits: GPT-3 only (davinci family); vignette text may be in the training data. One seeing-versus-doing paradigm.
agent_relevance: Vignette success hides brittle causal handling. Check the interventional distribution in code (G3, G5).

source: Jin et al. (2024) Can large language models infer causation from correlation? (Corr2Cause). ICLR 2024; arXiv 2306.05836
finding: 207,972-sample benchmark: given correlations among variables, decide whether a causal statement is valid. 17 LLMs were near or below random. Fine-tuned models reached 94.74 F1 but fell apart on paraphrases and renamed variables, so they learned surface patterns.
numbers: Positive label rate 18.57%. Best zero-shot F1 33.38 (BART MNLI), above GPT-4. Random uniform F1 20.38; always-majority accuracy 84.77. Most GPT-3 variants F1 about 15-29 with recall near 100 (predict valid too often). RoBERTa-Large MNLI fine-tuned 94.74 F1; on paraphrased test 39.29; after variable refactoring 62.30.
limits: Abstract graph statements, no real-world scenes. Zero-shot older models; reasoning models not in this version.
agent_relevance: Correlation to causation is a core S4 error. Rule: no causal claim from correlation unless an intervention or independence check was run in code.

source: Jin et al. (2024) CLadder: assessing causal reasoning in language models. arXiv 2312.04350
finding: 10K questions on Pearl's three rungs (association, intervention, counterfactual), with answers from an oracle causal engine. GPT-4 is only modestly above chance. A stepwise CausalCoT prompt adds 8.37 points. Models do worse on anti-commonsensical and nonsensical variable versions.
numbers: Vanilla GPT-4 62.03% overall; CausalCoT 70.40% (+8.37). Binary answers, so chance is 50%. On the earlier v1.0 data GPT-4 got 63.95 and CausalCoT 66.64 (+2.36). Many GPT-4 splits in the v1.5 table sit near 50-57%.
limits: Templated formal questions; no tool-checked inference tested.
agent_relevance: A stepwise prompt helps a little; exact calculation in code is safer.

source: Kiciman, Ness, Sharma & Tan (2024) Causal reasoning and large language models: opening a new frontier for causality. TMLR; arXiv 2305.00050
finding: Knowledge-based causal reasoning (not data-based): GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 beat earlier methods on several tasks but make unpredictable mistakes and are not robust.
numbers: Pairwise causal direction 97% (previous best 83%, Mosaic). Counterfactual benchmark 92% (20 points gain). Necessary and sufficient causes on 15 vignettes over 86%. Normality assessment 70%. In one test prompt engineering raised weighted accuracy about 5 points to 86.9%.
limits: Variable names carry meaning (altitude, temperature), and benchmark leakage cannot be excluded.
agent_relevance: LLMs hold causal priors from text but are weak at discovery from data. Use them to propose hypotheses and use code to test them.

source: Yiu, Kosoy & Gopnik (2023) Imitation versus innovation: what children can do that large language and language-and-vision models cannot (yet)? arXiv 2305.07666
finding: Children and adults both recognise and innovate tool uses; LLMs (GPT-3.5, text-davinci-003, Claude, FLAN-UL2) are good at typical uses and much weaker at picking a novel functional object. The paper also summarises blicket work: children learn causal overhypotheses from a few events and explore efficiently; LLMs given the same data in words did worse.
numbers: Common tool recognition: children (n=42, ages 3-7, mean 5.71) 88.4%, adults (n=30) 84.9%. Novel functional choice: children 85.2%, adults 95.7%. LLM scores are in a figure, not extracted.
limits: Position paper with a few tasks; LLM numbers not read in text.
agent_relevance: Frames LLMs as transmission engines. Supports putting the discovery loop (S4) in program code instead of expecting it from the model.

source: Qiu, Sha, Allen, Kim, Linzen & van Steenkiste (2026) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in large language models. arXiv 2503.17523
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs update beliefs poorly in a 5-round flight recommendation task and mostly stop improving after round 1. Fine-tuning them to copy a Bayesian assistant's predictions (Bayesian teaching) beats copying the true answers (oracle teaching), and the skill transfers to unseen domains (hotels, web shopping).
numbers: 624 simulated users; 100 new flight sets scored per round. Bayesian Assistant final-round accuracy 81%. Original Gemma, Llama and Qwen models score far lower (labelled values in the figure range roughly 36 to 53). Bayesian-tuned models agree with the Bayesian Assistant about 80% of the time. Exact per-model values not extracted.
limits: Preference learning, not causal discovery. Needs fine-tuning, which the schema does not use.
agent_relevance: Quantifies the LLM-to-Bayes gap. Since we cannot train, do the update in code (G5) and let the model supply likelihood judgments only.

source: GX-Chen, Lin, Samiei, Precup, Richards, Fergus & Marino (2025) Language agents mirror human causal reasoning biases. How can we help them think like scientists? COLM 2025; arXiv 2505.09614
finding: Blicket tests with LM agents (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1, Gemma3, Llama 3.x, QwQ). Agents infer disjunctive rules well but fail on conjunctive rules, even when the evidence for conjunctive is as strong or stronger. The bias persists across families, sizes and prompting, and grows with the number of objects. Agents look adult-like, not child-like. Exploration is inefficient, sometimes worse than random (Gemma3, DeepSeek-R1). Longer reasoning correlates with lower accuracy (p<0.05). Fix: sample many hypotheses as Python functions, reject duplicates to flatten the prior, then ask for actions that eliminate as many as possible.
numbers: Information gain correlates most strongly with final accuracy. GPT-4o explores best. Hypothesis sampling with 16, 32, 64 and 96 unique initial hypotheses reduces the disjunctive bias in the 8-object task, with accuracy rising with the number of unique hypotheses (values in figures, not extracted). Even with oracle exploration data GPT-4o keeps a disjunctive bias.
limits: Text-based blicket tasks only. Exact accuracy values are in figures that were not extracted.
agent_relevance: Most direct support for the agent: hypothesis sampling plus elimination in code beats default LLM inference on S4. Longer reasoning is not better (G1).

source: Alderete, Benthall, Xu & Xing (2026) Separable pathways for causal reasoning: how architectural scaffolding enables hypothesis-space restructuring in LLM agents. arXiv 2604.20039
finding: Extends blicket tests with a mid-task rule change that forces the hypothesis space to grow. Two scaffold parts: context graphs (typed state machine for exploration) and dynamic behaviours (monitor evidence and expand the hypothesis space at runtime). Context graphs raise reasoning quality after the switch (94% of the gain); dynamic behaviours detect regime change and stop premature commitment.
numbers: 1,085 trials in all. Raw accuracy in one table: base 96/110 (87.3%), context graphs 85/110 (77.3%), both parts 98/110 (89.1%); both vs context graphs alone Fisher exact p=0.015 (one-tailed). Context graphs alone were numerically below base, not significant, linked to an exactly-N trap (21.8% vs 10.9%). The contradiction detector DB4 had 100% sensitivity over 136 firings.
limits: Under-review preprint from a company; batches of 30 to 110 per arm; no independent replication.
agent_relevance: Matches our schema: a state machine plus a trigger that fires on a contradiction with the current model (G1, G2). Warns that structure alone can hurt without the trigger.

source: Samiei, Yiu, GX-Chen, Lin, Shen, Richards, Gopnik & Precup (2026) Human adults and LLMs as scientists: who benefits from active exploration? arXiv 2606.06464
finding: The conjunctive handicap in adults is largely a passive-evidence effect. When adults design their own tests in a nexiom (blicket-like) task they do well on conjunctive rules, though these need more tests. Passive observers and passive proposers (who plan tests but do not see outcomes) do worse. LLMs approach human accuracy but explore less efficiently and keep a conjunctive-disjunctive gap.
numbers: 306 Prolific adults (mean age 30.41). Mean tests, conjunctive vs disjunctive: average human 9.6 vs 6.4; top human 8.5 vs 3.8; GPT-5 10.2 vs 7.7. Mean actions: human 32.1 vs 20.8; GPT-5 26.2 vs 21.0. In conjunctive environments, object identification accuracy was 0.12 for passive proposers, 0.45 for passive observers and 0.69 for active explorers; rule accuracy 0.57, 0.69 and 0.82. Among average human adults 16% got both rule and objects wrong, another 16% got the rule but not the objects. GPT-5 and DeepSeek-reasoner reached near-perfect disjunctive accuracy.
limits: June 2026 preprint; online adults only; one task family.
agent_relevance: Doing the test yourself matters, so the agent should see its own test outcomes. Conjunctive structures need more tests; budget for them.

source: Gopnik & Wellman (2012) open issues and variability, from the review text
finding: The authors list open issues: the hypothesis space is vast, development is piecemeal, and individual children vary. In Liu et al. (2007) about 50 preschoolers did 20 to 30 false-belief tasks each; 65% passed more than 75% and 30% passed fewer than 25%, with only 3 children in between. They read such data as consistent with stable hypotheses at the child level.
numbers: Liu et al. 2007 figures as quoted in the review.
limits: These are the authors' own remarks. Independent critiques of Bayesian cognitive models (Jones & Love 2011; Marcus & Davis 2013) were not opened in this angle.
agent_relevance: Do not treat group-level Bayes fit as proof of mechanism; check behaviour per run.

source: Denison et al. (2013) discussion: competing explanations for variability
finding: Alternatives were considered: random responding, noisy maximizing, reinforcement-style probability matching, and social-pragmatic switching (children change an answer when the interviewer repeats a question). Experiments 2 to 4 rule out the first three; the authors accept that a pragmatic account can still explain part of the alternating pattern in Exp 1.
numbers: Exp 2: the noisy-max model needed 58% pure chance responding, which the authors call implausible. Exp 4: observed 68% vs 36% predicted by frequency matching.
limits: No test directly separates sampling from pragmatic switching. A 2025 paper on repeated risky choices was seen in a listing but not opened.
agent_relevance: Variability has two sources: honest uncertainty and conversational artefacts. Repeated prompting itself changes answers (G4).
